record.paper_title: Quo Vadis Strangeness? Strangeness — Open Questions
record.original_question: If quark-gluon plasma is produced in nuclear collisions, how are final-state hadrons produced from the deconfined phase, and which chemical-freeze-out scenario is correct: low-temperature hadronization with little subsequent change in hadron abundances, denser hadron production followed by confined-hadron chemical re-equilibration, or explosive continuous disintegration of the QGP into free-flowing particles?

evidence.quote: If quark-gluon plasma is produced in nuclear collisions, a major theoretical challenge is the understanding of the hadronization process. In principle, production and emission of particles can occur throughout the evolution of the dense matter fireball.
A sample of alternative evolution scenarios that could be responsible for the production of the final state hadrons includes:
If the hadronization temperature is low (say below 145MeV), it can be safely assumed that there will be little, if any, subsequent change in the hadron abundances.

If hadron production from the deconfined phase were to occur at conditions that are more dense (in terms of baryon density, or particle density in general, synonymous with higher temperature), chemical re-equilibration among confined final state hadrons should occur, erasing the eventual particle abundance signature of the primordial QGP phase; this is possibly the situation at AGS energies.

The possibility of explosive and continuous disintegration cannot be ruled out at present. In this scenario, beginning at high temperatures QGP phase decays successively by emission of free-flowing particles.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collision in which a deconfined phase of quarks and gluons (a quark–gluon plasma, QGP) is formed. The QGP fireball expands and cools, and eventually final-state hadrons are produced and stream freely to detectors. The "chemical freeze-out" is the stage at which inelastic processes cease so that hadron abundances become fixed.

Determine which of the following hadronization/chemical-freeze-out scenarios correctly describes the production of final-state hadrons from the deconfined phase in such collisions:

(a) Sudden hadronization at a low temperature (e.g. below roughly 145 MeV), after which hadron abundances undergo essentially no further change, so that the observed yields directly reflect the QGP at hadronization.

(b) Hadron production from the deconfined phase at higher density/temperature, followed by a phase of chemical re-equilibration among confined hadrons in a dense hadronic medium that erases the primordial QGP abundance signature.

(c) Explosive, continuous disintegration of the QGP into free-streaming particles distributed throughout the evolution of the fireball, with no sharply defined single freeze-out hypersurface.

Identify which scenario (if any) is realized in nuclear collisions, and characterize the kinematic/energy regime (e.g. AGS, SPS, RHIC, LHC) in which each scenario may apply.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work indicates that at RHIC and LHC the data favor sudden hadronization of a supercooled QGP, with chemical freeze-out essentially coincident with QGP breakup (scenario (a)/(c) hybrid). At lower AGS/SPS energies, hadronic re-equilibration (scenario (b)) is more plausible. More recent flavor-dependent and sequential freeze-out analyses suggest strange and light hadrons may freeze out at different temperatures, so a fully universal answer is still being refined.

status_evidence.title: Non-equilibrium Hadrochemistry in QGP Hadronization
status_evidence.snippet: Sudden hadronization of supercooled QGP supported; chemical freeze-out coincides with QGP breakup at RHIC.
status_evidence.claim: Supports scenario (a)/sudden hadronization at high collision energy.

status_evidence.title: Universal QGP Hadronization Conditions at RHIC and LHC
status_evidence.snippet: Universal hadronization conditions at RHIC and LHC are characterized.
status_evidence.claim: Single sudden hadronization scenario favored at high energies.

status_evidence.title: Sequential Strangeness Freeze-out
status_evidence.snippet: Strange hadrons freeze out earlier than light hadrons; flavor hierarchy.
status_evidence.claim: Indicates the simple single-freeze-out picture is being refined; not fully closed.
